pitch_detail.notes: Starts between two neighbouring lines, sharing its first moves with another route. A couple of thin moves lead to easier ground, then a ledge traverse up and right past a bush. Gear belay. A gentle leg warm-up.

Discontinuous cracks lead to a bulge with loose blocks under a thin, left-leaning lie-back bulge. Climb beneath it past a piton to a bolted belay on a small sloping ledge. Can be linked with pitch 1 on an 80 m rope, but the traverse brings rope drag and some simul-climbing.

Go straight up from the right side of the belay on easy unprotected face moves to a small ledge, then up a pleasant dihedral to a stance under a roof. Step left into a splitter (watch the looser blocks), climb it, then traverse right into the big dihedral to a bolt and on to a bolted belay around the bulge. Going straight through the roof is possible but unprotected.
Aim for the alcove and the steep overhanging dihedral, which climbs easier than it looks. Step right where it pinches, then continue to the tower. Linking with pitch 3 works but drags.
From the tower, a thin-hands splitter leads to a water-polished lie-back. Pass two big detached flakes, then finish on a bolted face sequence on the right wall. Birds may nest on the first flake.
Technical stemming and crimping up a bolted corner, a stiff test before the crux pitch above.

The crux. Stemming and crimping continue on smaller holds, then thin face moves curve up and left over a bulge, finishing at anchors beneath another dihedral. Strenuous and sensitive to temperature, so reach it before the sun does. Hidden jug crimps sit on and around the bulge near the sixth draw.
Three bolts then gear: more stemming on lower-quality, mossy rock, ending in an outstanding fingers-to-tips splitter. Gear belay at the top. Often linked with pitch 9.
A short, grubby crack that leans right and is climbed upside down, ending on a sloping ledge. Fixed nuts and slings at the top serve as a bail point.

Splitter hands for about 20 ft, then right on suspect thin flakes to a wide crack. Follow that through an overhang and around an exposed arete to a low-angle wide crack at the start of the summit ridge. A #4 is handy.

Follow the ridge over short blocks to the ledge below the highest right arete, where bolted anchors sit beneath the last pitch of the neighbouring route. Climb the fully bolted 5.11 arete or traverse right to a hand-crack splitter; both are fine.

review.changed: Wrote 11 pitches. Pitch 11 is graded only as 5.11 for the arete option so no grade token given. Rappel text gives bail advice, not a station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Variation start: begin up a neighbouring route, then cut right to the anchor of another line near the top at a good stance. Bolt-protected only.
Work right past a pair of bolts and merge with the original line, which follows a corner facing left. A roof pull, a few bolts, and a good crack lead to an anchor on a ledge.
Up and left over the buttress. Go past the mostly hanging rappel anchor and build your own anchor in the hand crack on the ledge.
Climb the buttress to the right at 5.10b past a few bolts, or take the hand crack (5.2) and scramble to the higher ledge anchor, which also links easily with pitch 3.
Bolts up a lovely face on perfect rock, cruxy in places. Bolt-protected only.
More bolts and more good climbing, though the rock gets a bit worse. Bolt-protected only.
Right, then left up the buttress. Enjoyable, but watch for loose blocks.
A very exposed arete to finish, protected by bolts only.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches. Rappel text is only "single 70", so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A low-angle, right-leaning hand crack that is mostly scrambling, with a little simul-climbing on a 60 m rope. Set up a gear belay in a small flake on the right, just under the first bolt of the neighbouring bolted dike.

The physical crux: a large roof. Reaching the lip is tricky and getting over it harder; a knee bar helps to set up a hand jam, and a small cam is worth saving for the lip. About 25 ft above, traverse left to a bolted belay near a dike.

Go directly to the first bolt, then hard left into an easily protected roof, which goes using a hidden jug. Continue in the crack left of the roof toward bolts two and three. The gear feels awkward but there is always enough: small and medium cams and nuts.
Easy and pleasant: step left whenever a crack ends while generally trending right toward the single crack through the brown overhang above.
Climb past three bolts to a small overhang, pull over it, then trend up and left to avoid a runout.
Three bolted pitches of sustained crimping up a vertical headwall, each between 5.11a and 5.11c depending on how you read the moves. Entirely bolt-protected; about 13 draws are needed.

Short, cruxy and well protected. The belay is followed by a hard move, then a leftward shuffle on small features to jugs, and back right to another bolted belay. Going straight right at the last bolt is harder; the alternative is a slabby, more exciting traverse once you have stood up above that bolt.
Over the obvious overhang, then up and left on easy ground about 30 ft to a bolt. Above that, sling chickenheads or run it out roughly 45 ft on easier climbing.
A left-facing corner leads to two bolts, then gear if you continue straight. The bolted belay lies further left and belongs to another route.

review.changed: Wrote 10 entries: P0 and P1-P10, with P5-P7 combined as the text does not separate them. Rappel text only says two 60 m ropes, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count 10 matches P1-P10 plus a P0 approach pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: From the flake hole, up a left-facing corner to a roof; a knee bar above your head and a lie-back to locks make the most awkward move of the route (about 5.11b). Then four bolts of 5.11c lead to 5.9 ground shared with another route, and a bolt out left under the roof to anchors.
Lie-back dihedral with bolts and gear, out a good roof and up a clean prow past a rappel anchor, then left through a little lie-back crux with a bolt to a pedestal belay.

The Question: up and right from the belay, boulder to the first bolt, clip the second, then fight an intense seam of holds at about 5.12 to a hand-jam pod. Then 5.11 splitter to a last 5.11- bolt and chains shared with a neighbouring route. A crack to the right bypasses this at 5.11.
Undercling right and lie-back down to face features (5.5) linking to good protection, then a 5.10 crack up and right to a good ledge.
The Green Flame: engaging crack climbing to a five-bolt seam through a green panel.

The Improbable Pitch: the furthest-right vertical dihedral, then intermittent moderate cracks in a long right-angled sweep to cool locks below a ledge with a high two-bolt anchor. No bolts, despite looking blank.

The Believer: five bolts of hard face climbing trend up and left into an intermittent crack, then two more bolts up and right reach a ledge anchor. The hardest micro-crimping on the route, about 5.12a when cold and notably harder when hot.
Right past an old pin, up a left-facing dihedral to a stance, then out onto the right arete and back into the dihedral where it opens to fingers, ending at a two-bolt anchor.

The cleanest crack above the belay to a double hand-crack roof right of a hanging block. Stand on the block, clip high bolts left, then underclinging bolts to a double arete and shallow dihedral. Gear up and left to a two-bolt anchor.

Wide Asleep: an undercling wide roof visible from the valley. Climb left, reverse the exit of a neighbouring route and work out the wide flake. Easy but intimidating, with a three-bolt pump finish to a stance with chains.
Epic: five bolts above the belay, then thin intermittent cracks and more bolts angling up and right. Take a seated rest, then make the last tough pulls past a bolt, with gear at the top of a pillar.

Cherry on top: easy lie-back to a three-bolt crux off a ledge, then thin cracks up and right joining the final pitch of a neighbouring route to top out the ridge. At 45 m, rappel to the ledge and scramble back to the main rap line.

review.changed: Wrote all 12 pitches. Descent lists 12 rappels loosely, not as a clean station-by-station table, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Text says pitch 3 can be bypassed at 5.11; stored grade 5.13a matches the 5.13a pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a low-angle left-facing ramp in a recess, 100 ft left of the red dihedral. Follow low-angle corners aiming steadily up and slightly right; avoid loose rock.
Gentle ramps lead up and right, then a little left toward the white corner that forms the left edge of the cracked wall. Belay at a scooped ledge.

Take the right-most blocky corner up to a wide crack in a flake. Once on the broken pillar, move left into a hanging hand crack, then left again beneath a chockstone and bolt to a rail of jugs. The belay is on a slim stance under a thin corner.

A superb finger crack up a left-facing corner for 45 ft ends in a bombay chimney where you can rest with no hands. Turn around and leave to the right through the notch on a great jug, reaching the upper dihedral. Small offset nuts help; the bolt at the exit keeps the rope off a worrying edge.

Up the corner with twin finger cracks, passing the roof crux with the left arete and a single right-hand fingerlock. Easier ground follows, going up and right along a crack system to a perch on the left past a bolt. You can skip the crux by going around the corner on the left under the roof.
Many cracks to choose from: up the groove left, step right to a rib trending left after the first of two bolts, to a belay under the leftmost bolted undercling corner.
Up a rotten groove on the right, step left at a bolt into the corner, lie-back past a large undercling flake, and step left past a bolt at the top to anchors. Bolts were added in the lower corner.
Follow overlapping corners trending slightly right to a rappel station under a blank face. Technical and varied.

Step right into a bolted corner and follow its steps up and right toward a massive table-top block. Skip the thin corner leading to it: instead traverse left along a rotten handrail for 30 ft to a small hand crack that gains a large ledge.
Up the chute corner on the left, then up and left past fins and blocks toward the finishing tower to a perch above a large detached flake.

A short crux right off the belay passes a bolt; after that, splitter cracks and corners lead directly to the cozy ledge under the summit tower. The last pitch of the red dihedral comes in from the right.

Scramble right around a balanced block and up pillars to a bolt, aiming for a mini hand-crack roof on the right (rotten band; careful). Pull into a flared finger-to-hands splitter leading to the summit. Anchors sit below the lip.

review.changed: Wrote all 12 pitches. Descent says anchored raps of no more than 35 m, not a station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A splitter finger crack, with a crimp and a stem past a pinch, then the main dihedral curves left to a belay ledge scattered with loose stones.
The Green Dihedral: a dihedral full of finger cracks, passing a ledge and continuing to the very top of the pillar.

A short, steep finger crack straight up is the crux and gives way to easier terrain. Next comes a poorly protected 5.7 R slab, then corners trending up and right to a small ledge on the right. Skip the bigger ledge on the left.

The Yellow Jamcrack: climb a stepped finger crack toward a lichen-spotted clean corner of 4-5 inch width. Deep jams lead to a short offwidth move, then up and right on a flaky finger crack to a crescent belay ledge.

The right-trending crescent ramp leads to a scrappy right-facing corner. Move 15 ft to the left into a boxy recess beside a giant pedestal, climb a few more fifth-class steps, and stop where the slope relents.
Wind between hanging blocks up to the crest of the buttress.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches. No rappel text (walk-off descent).

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the glacier top and take either of two clean corners, the left being easier and the right better protected, for about 20 ft to reach the green wall. Moderate cracks then lead out left to a bolted ledge belay.
Follow a snow ramp or dirt and rock left, then up 3rd-class ledges to the bolted belay at the foot of the giant corner system. A seasonal snow patch may call for boots in early season.
The long, enjoyable corner to a belay out left.
The Yellow Leaf: step back right and continue up the same corner.
Walk the ledges left to the bolted belay.
Stems and Seeds: two bolts take you up and right to a large ledge, a third bolt precedes about 30 ft of thin laser-cut crack, and four more bolts reach the belay.

The Cali Connector: about 35 ft of offset rail, then a desperate reach left to a crimp rail. Continue up and left around a steep arete on square-cut edges, finishing with a tricky last move into the belay at the foot of the next corner.
The Cola Corner: the huge corner for the full length.
Straight up moderate cracks and face holds; in the last 15 ft cut right onto easy ledges, then back left to the belay.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches. Descent gives a rap tip for the second rappel but no full station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Up and slightly right past three bolts to the fourth, on a bulge. Cross the bulge and pass five more bolts, reaching an anchor on a spacious ledge. A 60 m rope barely gets there. A flake between bolts one and two takes small cams.
Face climbing on twelve bolts to an anchor beneath a small tree. A link-up goes past the tree to join another route at its second bolt, at about 5.4 with medium cams.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Rappel text is a count only (3 raps, two 60 m ropes), so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the flake and crack to a small ledge under a left-facing corner. The corner thins from hands to tips and then widens again. At the cleft, one last bouldery step reaches a belay on the main wall, where a hand-crack system begins.
A steep hand-crack system with switches between cracks and several roofs, ending with a step right to the large chockstone capping the chimney. Belay on the party ledge. A burly pitch for its grade.

Shift the belay roughly 10 ft right, to where a thin hand crack leads into a big right-facing corner. This technical corner offers good stances up to a sloping ledge under a roof. Easiest is to exit right over a flake and use a hand crack, ledges and a thin crack, then a short move back left onto a small ledge.
Cracks and solid blocks everywhere; trend left up the face and belay in a big sloping alcove at the foot of a headwall with flared splitters.

Above the belay, ascend the corner, then shift right to the narrow hand crack that cuts the headwall; it feels easier than it appears. An exposed slab follows, reaching a good ledge on the ridge. About 20 m of airy ridge remains to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches. No rappel text (descent is a 3rd-class gully).

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a moderate ramp, step right to a nice face and edge up to an anchor. Six bolts plus a couple of cams.

Critical Mass: step left into a lovely crack that pinches to tips yet is offset at the crux, so lie-backing works. Look for knobs. Pass the intermediate rappel anchor, continue up the crack and traverse right to the anchor. Five bolts plus gear.
Particle Accelerator: a seam leads to a mantle onto a dike stance, then the corner, then a traverse out the roof to an anchor on the arete. Eight bolts and a single rack.
Quantum Leap: bolts and knobs lead left to another beautiful crack, and the top has a cruxy leftward traverse to a ledge anchor. Four bolts plus gear.
Ow My Buckyballs: sport-bolted climbing winding back and forth around the arete on seams and edges. Twelve bolts.
Up the corner, then right and take your pick of cracks to a ledge. Two bolts and a single rack.
Chimney to a ledge on the upper left, then scramble onward to the dramatic summit. One bolt and a single rack.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches. Descent is seven single 70 m rappels described only in outline, so no rappel table. No crux flagged since text names none.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin up a splitter crack in a right-facing corner. It is harder than it looks and a little flared inside, which makes the jams technical. Belay on a semi-hanging stance on blocks.

Route-finding is easy: stay in the continuous corner. The crux follows the guillotine flake, with sustained finger and off-finger splitter, then a good rest and a long stretch of 5.10 hands to a semi-hanging stance.
More perfect hands. Near the top, two imposing roofs climb easier than they look.
Take any logical line to the mid-height ledge, depending on where you belayed; watch for loose rock near the walk-off ledge.
About 100 ft to the left of where the previous pitch ended, find twin railroad-track splitter cracks and follow them to any good ledge. Terrain eases here.
Good crack systems continue until the angle eases.
Roughly 300 ft of 3rd and 4th class scrambling reaches the summit block, which needs one low-5th-class move that must be reversed on descent.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries (P7 is scrambling). Descent mentions two rappels but no station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A few pitons can be seen in an incipient crack from the ground. Good gear low down plus well-driven pins, ending on a ledge on top of a pillar. Do not put gear beneath the downward-facing flake: it makes a handy jug once the hard part is over but is not trustworthy.
Continue up the left-facing corner, using holds and knobs on the arete, to a good right-slanting stance.
Easy opening moves, then a punchy finger crack leading to sustained splitter climbing, corner changes and mini roofs to a good stance out left.

Continue up the same crack system; cracks out left seam out, so go straight up the splitters. An endurance pitch with some flared jams, easing higher, to the huge walk-off ledge. Watch loose blocks on the easy ground leading to it.
Roughly 100 ft left of where the previous pitch topped out, find twin railroad-track splitter cracks and follow them to any good ledge. Terrain eases.
Good crack systems upward until the angle relents.
Around 300 ft of 3rd and 4th class scrambling reaches the summit block; one low-5th-class move gains the top and must be reversed.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries (P7 is scrambling). Descent mentions two rappels, not a station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A crack just to the left of a deep chimney on the southeast side, trending left up easy ramps. Many belay options.
Continue up rambling terrain to the foot of the headwall splitter. Watch rope drag among the many options.
Up to the big ledge at the foot of the headwall splitter.

Head for the bush at the foot of a wide crack that curves left (a #5 helps). Climb the left-facing flake to an awkward flared pod, which is the crux of this pitch, then traverse right on strong holds and follow the crack to a stance below the thin-hands splitter.
Straight up the sustained splitter, thin hands turning to off-fingers, with the angle easing near the big ledge on the spire shoulder.
Move the belay on easy terrain to one of three cracks leading to the summit block; the right-most is easiest to climb and protect.
Straight up a wide right-facing corner, starting as a #5 crack and narrowing to hands, then any hand crack to the summit block. Short but powerful.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches. Descent is a scramble with one 35 m rappel, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the crack and chimney system to the second ledge system, which offers a way left.

Take the right-angling crack system, now hand-crack size, diagonally up and right across the south face. It ends in a brief trough hidden behind a triangular pinnacle; set the belay near the far end. Splitting here keeps rope drag down.
Up the south face and southeast arete to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches from the feet-length breakdown; the text gives no per-pitch grades. No rappel text (walk-off).

pitch_detail.notes: Some rotten rock at the start gives way to an easy crack. Traverse the face right at a bolt to the next crack system, climb to a roof, then follow bolts up the face to an anchor on a great ledge.

Take the right-hand corner. A line of bolts goes up and then leftward to an arete. After the last bolt, continue on the face, then move left into a corner that faces left. A roof caps it; undercling rightward to the stance.
Back left to the corner and up a little, then left into another corner and again left to a crescent crack with a crux transfer at the top. Wild stemming to a roof and belay. Can be wet after storms.
Wander up and right to a high bolt, downclimb, and dyno right to the belay ledge.

A long run of good corner cracks, with two bolts guarding a blank section and two more where the crack closes. At the roof, traverse across to the stance, downclimbing once or twice; keep the second climber in mind.
A fine hand crack.
Headwall splitters; a traverse left to one, then aim left into the left corner higher. Slightly fresh rock.
Finger crack straight up beside an arete; higher, take the right-hand hand crack (hidden from the belay) at a junction to the top-out ledge.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches. Rappel text is brief (fixed anchors, two ropes), so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Shared with a neighbouring route, with the crux in the first 30 ft. Save a #4 for a short wide stretch in the middle. Chippy but fun, with improving rock. Belay on the big ledge below the pitch 2 bolt. The original start (5.10b) climbs thin hands to wide crack out of a small tree and needs larger gear.
One bolt guards face moves up to a flake. The crack then leads to a flake rail that leaves to the left. Build the anchor on a good stance on the left, beneath a corner that faces left.
Go up the corner, up and right, and clip a bolt that protects the move into a higher corner. The flake that looks suspect is in fact solid. Trend up and left to a good anchor stance.

The money pitch: a lovely corner that changes from right-facing to left-facing partway. Bridge leftward beyond a bolt onto a ramp; a second bolt guards the moves into a finger crack that rejoins the hand crack on the roof's right. The belay is one bolt plus a slung flake.
More crack climbing, with enough face holds that nothing wide is needed. Near the top, step into a shallow right-facing corner holding a finger crack, ending on a good stance.
A rightward-trending left-facing corner to a big ledge.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches (P1 uses the main 5.9 start, original 5.10b start in notes). Descent is two rappels in outline without lengths, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Start with a chunky corner leading into a hand crack within a chimney. Pass an intermediate anchor and cross a moderate slab to the right, arriving at a large stance with a bolted anchor under the next pitch. Rock is somewhat crumbly.

The money pitch. Climb the corner's left face until you can work around a roof on the left to reach a beautiful angled crack on a clean face. Higher up, crack switches up and left reach a bolted ledge anchor.

The Lasso of Truth: at a bolt, step left into a lie-back, then follow intermittent corners and bolts up a face of high-quality rock, through a crystal band, to a bolted stance. Five bolts plus small gear to a #1.
The Slot: fingers up the slot's left-hand side, then step right and keep following the corner. A bolted anchor waits on a decent, if slopey, stance.
Steep hands to a right-facing corner of hands to fingers, then ramble to the summit ridge and anchor where you like.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches. Descent is two rappels in outline, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: If the ice does not reach the ground, a variation on the right passes a piton bail sling and climbs a 20 ft left-facing corner that can be unprotected when the ice is thin; a fixed nut can be clipped at the top. The crux is higher, moving onto water ice on the left, where thin ice may mean a big pendulum fall. Grade depends on how the ice forms.
Up ice past a small bulge and onto slabbier ground before it steepens again. Anchor in solid ice.
Grade varies with variation. Climb to an anchor on the big snow slope to bring up partners, then hike to the next ice step.
The slabby first step (WI2) then part-way up the final slabby ice (about WI2+). Go as far as possible.
Finish the remaining ice up to the top and belay off the tree.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches; no lengths or anchors given. Rappels not described.
review.other_findings: Text says the route is more like 700-800 ft than the stated 1000 ft; avalanche-prone slopes above.

pitch_detail.notes: One bolt 10 ft up marks a clean left-slanting diagonal crack, well protected with small to medium cams. A good warm-up.

The Superbloom Crack: start in the right crack about 20 ft, transfer left into the main crack for 30 ft, then out left into an offset finger crack. Finger locks, lie-backing and sequences between tiny gear (offset nuts, tiny cams); two bolts protect the final crux moves. Too long for a 70 m rappel by 20 ft.
Reach the top of the big ledge on the right, then follow a clean ramp that leans up and left for 100 ft, with good gear along the way.

The Green Corner: enter with some chimney technique and face holds, then precise, laser-cut climbing protected by tiny cams. Exit left past the steep arete with two bolts and finish with 40 ft of easy climbing to the big ledge.

Shift the belay along the ledge to the foot of a dirty green right-facing corner. Climb it for 20 ft, then the right-facing flake for 40 ft (5.8). Set a cam, then go left onto the obvious vertical bolted face for 30 ft to a comfortable ledge.

Climb the corner crack for 20 ft, then when it gets hard, transfer to another crack on the right for 20 ft to a stance on sharp spikes beneath a short vertical wall. A vertical slot there takes finger-size cams that protect the reachy move to a white bucket flake. Right of that, easier climbing leads to the final bolted belay.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches. Rappel text says 80 m rope needed, with no station list, so no rappel table.

skip_reasons.ca_dark_star_4: low confidence: loose text, count conflict
